title: The Sleep Science Mystery
synopsis: A student journalist investigates why classmates feel exhausted and learns to separate evidence from viral health claims.

chapters.title: The Sleep Challenge
paragraphs: Student reporter Sana noticed that half her classmates arrived yawning. A popular video claimed that a special drink could replace several hours of sleep. Sana wanted to test the claim for the school newspaper, but her science teacher asked her to begin with reliable evidence.

Sana interviewed classmates about their schedules without collecting private medical information. She found late homework, long commutes, noisy bedrooms and phones used well past bedtime. The causes were varied, and none could be solved by a miracle drink.

chapters.title: The Viral Promise
paragraphs: The drink's advertisement used scientific-looking charts without naming a study. Sana checked the source and discovered that the graph had been copied from an unrelated survey. The numbers looked impressive until she read the labels.
She learned that anecdotes and advertisements were not the same as controlled research. A claim about replacing sleep would need strong evidence, especially when teenagers' health was involved.

chapters.title: The Library Search
paragraphs: With the librarian's help, Sana read guidance from public-health organizations about regular sleep schedules, evening light and the importance of adequate sleep. She wrote down what the sources actually said and what they did not say.

Her teacher reminded her that people with persistent sleep problems should seek professional advice. Sana included that distinction in her article rather than promising that one routine would work for everyone.

chapters.title: A Week of Small Changes
paragraphs: The class tried a voluntary 'quiet evening' project: planning homework earlier, reducing unnecessary late-night messages and agreeing not to shame anyone who could not participate. They did not collect individual sleep data or award prizes.
Some students said they felt more rested. Others had responsibilities at home that made changes difficult. Sana refused to present the project as proof of a medical treatment.

chapters.title: The Editor's Question
paragraphs: The newspaper editor asked for a dramatic headline: 'One Trick Ends Tiredness Forever.' Sana argued for a less exciting but more accurate title. They settled on 'Why Our Class Is Tired — and What Evidence Suggests'.

The article described different pressures on students, quoted credible guidance and encouraged anyone with ongoing concerns to speak with a healthcare professional. It also questioned the drink's unsupported marketing.

chapters.title: The Morning After
paragraphs: The article sparked a discussion about homework deadlines and late-night group chats. Teachers adjusted one recurring assignment schedule, while students agreed to send nonurgent messages earlier.

Sana still yawned during first period now and then. She did not consider that a failure. Her real success was teaching readers to ask a better question whenever a health claim sounded too good to be true: 'Where is the evidence?'
